title: Don't let them distract you
hookLine: let neither wealth nor children distract you from remembering Allah (63:9)

lines: THE PHONE BUZZES ON THE SHELF.
cards: A parent stands in prayer. Behind them, a toddler narrates a cartoon at full volume. The phone on the shelf buzzes: a client, an invoice, the bank.
Somewhere in the second unit, the parent realizes they've been planning dinner. None of these things are bad. The child is loved.
The work feeds the child. That's exactly what makes them so good at pulling attention away. After its warnings, Surah Al-Munafiqun turns to the believers and names those two pulls.

teach.b: Pickthall: "O ye who believe! Let not your wealth nor your children distract you from remembrance of Allah."
The verb is tulhikum, from the root l-h-w, the same root as lahw, the amusement we met in Surah Al-Hadid two weeks ago.
Distraction and amusement are one family: whatever fills your attention so completely that something more important slips out. And notice what the verse names. Not sins.
Wealth and children, two things the Qur'an elsewhere calls the adornment of worldly life. The danger isn't in them. It's in how easily they take up the whole field of view.
Surah At-Takathur says it in one line: the rivalry for more distracts you, until you visit the graves. Same root, same pull. Then verse ten turns urgent.

teach.h: IF ONLY I HAD A LITTLE MORE TIME.
teach.b: Spend from what God has provided, before death comes to one of you and he says: my Lord, if only you'd give me a little more time, I would give in charity and be among the righteous.
Verse eleven answers: God does not delay a soul when its term has come. So the verse doesn't say: have less, love less.
It says: remember through it. The parent doesn't stop being a parent in prayer. The worker doesn't stop working.
But somewhere in the noise there's a thread back to God, and the verse asks believers not to let it drop. Those who do, it says, are the losers.

how: Muslims are taught to pray with presence of heart, and some silence phones and choose a quiet place; 63:9–11 is recited as a reminder to give in charity before death comes.

o: the rivalry for more, which distracts you
counting your blessings one by one
the greed of a soul that won't share

games.q: distraction in Al-Munafiqun — tap the pairs.
p: the root of amusement and distraction
if only a little more time

s: the verse calls wealth and children sinful
it names them as pulls on attention, not as sins.
the verb for distract shares a root with lahw, amusement
tulhikum and lahw both come from l-h-w.
verse eleven says God delays a soul when its term comes
it says God does not delay a soul when its term has come.

games.q: death comes to someone who never got around to giving. what does he say, in verse ten?
o: my Lord, if only you'd give me a little more time, I would give in charity.
my children will give for me.
games.why: he asks for a little more time to give and be righteous; verse eleven says no soul is delayed when its term comes.

practice: Put your phone in another room, or face down and silent, out of reach. If you pray, pray your next prayer this way; if not, simply sit without it for now.
Each time your mind runs to the screen, the inbox, the next errand, name the pull gently and come back to the breath.

wordCard.voice: Takathur: the rivalry for more, named in Surah At-Takathur as the same pull Surah Al-Munafiqun warns wealth and children can become. Today's word.

orig.say: laa TUL-hi-kum am-WAA-lu-kum wa laa aw-LAA-du-kum
orig.note: Arabic: let not your wealth nor your children distract you. tulhi is from l-h-w.

carryVoice: Your line: remember through it all. The noise doesn't have to win. See you tomorrow.

sources.q: O ye who believe! Let not your wealth nor your children distract you from remembrance of Allah.

sources.ref: Qur'an 63:10–11 (spend before death; no soul delayed)
Qur'an 18:46 (wealth and children, the adornment of worldly life)
